_____________________________________________________________________________

September 30, 2026

Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Esq., Secretary
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
888 First Street, N.E.
Washington, D.C. 20426

Re:     2028 Expansion Project
        Docket No. PF26-5-000
        Draft Resource Reports 1 – 13

Contains Critical Energy Infrastructure and Privileged Information that requires
special treatment pursuant to 18 C.F.R. §§ 388.112 and 388.113

Dear Ms. Reese:

On January 20, 2026, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (Commission or
FERC) issued approval for Great Basin Gas Transmission Company’s (Great Basin) to
utilize the prefiling process for its proposed 2028 Expansion Project (Project). Pursuant
to 18 CFR 157.21(f)(10) of the Commission’s regulations, Great Basin submits the draft
resource reports prepared in accordance with 18 C.F.R. § 380.12. Landowner and
Stakeholder lists are also provided. Great Basin is not providing a draft Resource Report
13 because the Project does not include construction of new liquefied natural gas (LNG)
facilities or the recommissioning of an LNG facility.

Great Basin has provided certain information that is regarded as either Privileged or
Critical Energy Infrastructure Information as defined in 18 C.F.R. §§ 388.112 and 388.113
of the Commission’s regulations. Such information has been labeled appropriately. This
information is provided in Volumes III and IV. Great Basin requests that these Volumes
be accorded privileged and confidential treatment under 18 C.F.R. §§ 388.112.

Please contact Great Basin’s counsel, John Paul Floom (703) 549-8606, Anthony Sassi
(702) 364-3357, or the undersigned (702) 876-7384 for questions about the CEII or
privileged status of the material that Great Basin is submitting as such.

Very truly yours,

/s/   Frank J. Maglietti, Jr.
Frank J. Maglietti Jr.
Vice President/General Manager

c       David Swearingen, FERC



                                    8350 S. Durango Drive | Las Vegas, NV 89113 | GreatBasinGTC.com

1.0 General Project Description
1.1   Introduction

Great Basin Gas Transmission Company (Great Basin) is filing an application for a Certificate of Public
Convenience and Necessity (Application) and Authority for Abandonment with the Federal Energy
Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission) under Section 7(c) and Section 7(b) of the Natural Gas
Act (NGA) and Part 157, Subpart A of the Commission’s Regulations (18 Code of Federal Regulations
[CFR] Part 157), as amended, to construct, operate, and maintain its 2028 Expansion Project (Project). The
Project consists of approximately 207 miles of new 48-inch diameter lateral pipeline (48-inch Lincoln
Lateral or Lincoln Lateral) and approximately 25 miles of smaller diameter lateral pipelines (Project
Laterals) as well as pressure limiting stations (PLSs) and other appurtenant facilities located in Churchill,
Humboldt, Lyon, Pershing, and Storey counties, Nevada. In addition, the Project also includes the
construction and operation of one new compressor station (Jungo Compressor Station) located in Humboldt
County, Nevada. The Project will provide an additional 948,876 dekatherms per day (Dth/d) of firm
transportation capacity to various delivery points to meet growing natural gas demand in northern Nevada.
Approximately 77 percent of the Project’s pipelines will be collocated with Great Basin’s existing pipeline,
other utilities, and roadways. After the Project is placed in service and is operational for approximately one
year, in 2030, Great Basin plans to abandon in place approximately 124 miles of its existing 16-inch
diameter pipeline (16-inch Mainline) and approximately 10 miles of its existing 8-inch diameter pipeline
(8-inch Gabbs Lateral) in Churchill, Humboldt, Lyon, Pershing, and Washoe counties, Nevada.
Additionally, at the existing Rye Patch and Lovelock Compressor Station sites all compressor-related
facilities will be abandoned by removal. The approximate 134 miles of pipeline to be abandoned, mostly
installed in the 1960s, and the two compressor stations will no longer be necessary to provide the Project
and existing contracted firm capacity.

Once all applicable permits, approvals, and authorizations are obtained, Great Basin plans on beginning
construction of the Project in late 2027 or upon receipt of authorizations. Great Basin’s target Project in-
service date is November 1, 2028.

This draft Resource Report 1 – General Project Description (Resource Report 1) was prepared in
compliance with the Commission’s regulations concerning Environmental Reports (ERs) for NGA Section
7(b) and Section 7(c) applications, under 18 CFR 380.3 and 380.12, (2024), and the FERC Guidance
Manual for Environmental Report Preparation (FERC 2017). Resource Report 1 describes the following:
Project design, Project purpose and need, Project facilities, procedures for construction and restoration,
future plans, required permits and authorizations, stakeholder outreach, and cumulative impact assessment
areas.

The Project is described in more detail in the following sections. Supplemental Tables and Drawings are
provided in Appendix 1.A. A Project overview map (Figure 1.B-1, General Project Location Map)
showing the Project route and the existing pipeline and compressor stations Great Basin plans to abandon
is included in Appendix 1.B (Figures). This draft Resource Report 1 will be further refined as Project
design advances, and additional information is available.

1.2     Facilities Proposed for Construction or Modification

1.2.1    Purpose and Need

Consistent with Commission policy, Great Basin conducted open seasons to determine the level of interest
for incremental firm transportation capacity from Great Basin’s interconnect with Ruby Pipeline north of
Winnemucca, Nevada, to downstream points of demarcation where custody of the gas is transferred from
the Project to the Project Shipper (Delivery Points). Following these open seasons, Great Basin executed
at least 20-year precedent agreements with ten parties that agree to execute Transportation Service
Agreements (TSAs) for the Project capacity (Project Shippers) of 948,876 Dth/d of incremental firm
capacity, to be available by November 1, 2028. Although the contracted firm capacity must be available at
the Project’s in-service date, Great Basin expects the delivery to vary from the Project Shippers demands
are fully implemented to their contracted Project capacity. Great Basin’s purpose and need for the Project
is to: 1) meet growing natural gas demand in northern Nevada by adding firm capacity of 948,876 Dth/d by
November 1, 2028, 2) enhance the reliability of Great Basin’s existing natural gas infrastructure, and 3)
design the system to handle the variability of Shippers’ needs.
The Project will transport natural gas from a new point on Great Basin’s system where gas can be delivered
onto Great Basin’s system. (Receipt Point) adjacent to Great Basin’s current Receipt Point with Ruby
Pipeline at Opal Valley near Winnemucca, Nevada to the southeast Tahoe Reno Industrial Center (TRIC)
area, southwest of Fernley, Nevada near the border between Storey and Lyon Counties, Nevada. The
Project includes twelve new Shipper Delivery Points (two Project Shippers have two Delivery Points each)
and three new PLSs connecting to existing lateral pipelines along the Project route.

Open seasons conducted by Great Basin and the resultant executed precedent agreements demonstrate the
demand for natural gas and the need for increased system capacity. The open seasons are summarized
below 1.

On March 20, 2024, Great Basin announced a Non-Binding Open Season during which it would consider:
1) requests from both prospective and Existing Shippers for new or additional firm transportation capacity
beginning in 2027 through 2030, 2) non-binding indications of interest in turning back capacity from the
Wadsworth or Owyhee Receipt Points 2, and 3) requests from Existing Shippers for changes to delivery
points or delivery point quantities under existing TSAs where the Shipper is seeking no additional capacity.
Great Basin received non-binding bids for firm capacity and continued to receive interest for additional
firm capacity.

Based on this requested need, Great Basin posted Notice of a Binding Open Season from January 28, 2025
to April 30, 2025, to confirm market support for the Project. The Binding Open Season indicated that each
participating Project Shipper would be required to execute a firm transportation service agreement for a
minimum of 20 years at an incremental rate dependent on actual contracted capacity. The Binding Open
Season was extended to May 28, 2025. Additionally, Great Basin posted a Notice of Supplemental Binding
Open Season to confirm additional market support from June 6 through June 16, 2025, and a Second
Supplemental Binding Open Season with a revised incremental rate from November 11, 2025 through
November 26, 2025. Through the Second Supplemental Binding Open Season, Great Basin executed at

in 1964 in Churchill, Humboldt, Lyon, Pershing, and Washoe counties; as well as two existing compressor
stations in Pershing County, Nevada. These abandoned facilities will no longer be required to deliver the
total contracted firm capacity, inclusive of existing firm capacity and incremental Project firm capacity,
once the Project is placed in service. The replacement of existing facilities with new, more efficient, and
modern facilities will enhance safety and system reliability for Great Basin’s Existing Shippers with
capacity for delivery downstream of the Ruby Pipeline Receipt Point and enable Great Basin to meet the
increased demand of Project Shippers that have executed at least 20-year firm transportation capacity
precedent agreements. Great Basin requests that the Commission allow Great Basin to abandon these
facilities in 2030, to allow it to operate its new system and provide service to all Great Basin Shippers for
approximately one year before beginning abandonment of the existing pipelines, compressor stations and
appurtenant facilities.

originate at a new interconnect with Ruby Pipeline in Humboldt County, Nevada, approximately 20 miles
north-northeast of Winnemucca, Nevada, at 48-inch Lincoln Lateral (LI) MP LI 5-0.0. The 48-inch Lincoln

approximately 25 miles. Six Project Laterals will originate from locations along the 48-inch Lincoln

MAOP of 1,440 psig. Construction of the 48-inch Lincoln Lateral and Project Laterals will use the

Compressor Station

The Jungo Compressor Station will be built to meet contracted pressures on the 48-inch Lincoln Lateral at
the points of delivery. In addition, a booster compressor station will be constructed at the site to enable the
delivery of gas from the existing 16-inch Mainline to be discharged into the 48-inch Lincoln Lateral. This
will allow for future abandonment of the 16-inch Mainline downstream of the Jungo Compressor Station.
The Jungo Compressor Station will be constructed within a single site consisting of approximately 75.2-
acres of privately-owned land, that will be fully enclosed with a six-foot-high chain-link security fence

The Jungo Compressor Station will include the following main facilities:

    •    Four Solar Turbines Mars 100 gas-turbine/centrifugal-compressor packages (12,624 horsepower
         each) (Mars 100 Units). The Mars 100 Units will compress the natural gas arriving via the 48-inch
         Lincoln Lateral and discharge at about 1,100 psig. Each turbine/compressor will be fully enclosed
         in a lean modular building. These will be operated on a 3+1 basis, meaning three units will be
         operating and one will be available as a back-up for redundancy to ensure reliability.
    •    Two Solar Turbines Centaur 40 gas-turbine/centrifugal-compressor packages (3,721 horsepower
         each) (Centaur 40 Units). The Centaur 40 Units will compress natural gas arriving via the 16-inch
         Mainline and discharge into the new 48-inch Lincoln Lateral. Each turbine/compressor will be
         fully enclosed in a lean modular building. These will be operated on a 1+1 basis, meaning one unit
         will be operating and one will be available as a back-up to ensure reliability.

Auxiliary equipment for each Solar Turbines compressor unit includes:

     •   Combustion air inlet ductwork with filters;
     •   Exhaust stack;
     •   Lube oil cooler;
     •   Process gas cooler;
     •   Station piping;
     •   Blowdown stacks for suction header, discharge header, and unit depressurization;
     •   Axial separator on compressor inlet; and
     •   Condensate tank.

Additional equipment includes:

    •    Filter-separators between the pipeline and the compressor suction header;
    •    Three enclosed instrument air compressor packages (electric motor driven);
    •    Two Local Equipment Rooms (power distribution centers) will be installed for the four Mars 100
         Units. A third Local Equipment Room will be installed for the two Centaur 40 Units; and
    •    Two methane capture skids will be installed for the four Mars 100 units and a third skid for the
         two Centaur 40 units. Solar Turbines names these skids “Catch4”. These skids capture natural
         gas leakage from the compressor seals and re-compress the leaked gas back into the system, rather
         than venting to atmosphere.

Support facilities include:

Receipt Point and Delivery Points

A Receipt Point and multiple Delivery Points will be constructed at interconnections with incoming or
outgoing gas supplies. These locations allow for measurement and control of natural gas flowing in and
out of the system, and typically include filtration, metering, regulation, and communication equipment for
remote monitoring and operation. Some Delivery Points may have a gas heater upstream of the regulation.
Sites will have an awning type structure (e.g., 8’x 4’) to protect equipment from the sun, will have a
permanent access road, and will be fully enclosed with a six-foot-high chain-link fence topped with three
strands of barbed wire, angled outward, for security purposes. Lighting will be addressed on a site-by-site
basis. Generally downward-directed low-intensity lights will be used for site illumination as necessary.
Lighting can be set up for manual turn-on with manual or timed turn-off. Motion sensitive lighting can be
triggered by wildlife which makes it undesirable.

The 48-inch Lincoln Lateral will have one Receipt Point at the Lincoln Lateral Interconnect to receive gas
from Ruby Pipeline. The Project has twelve Delivery Points to provide natural gas to Project Shippers as
listed above in Table 1.2-4.

Pressure Limiting Stations (PLSs)

The Project includes installation of three new PLSs to reduce the pressure of natural gas as it flows from
the 48-inch Lincoln Lateral into Great Basin’s existing laterals with smaller diameters and lower MAOP’s.
Both the Lovelock PLS (located at the existing Lovelock Compressor Station) and the Eagle Ridge PLS
(adjacent to existing aboveground facilities) will be located at currently disturbed areas. The Gabbs Lateral
PLS will be a new aboveground facility. A fourth PLS consists of the replacement of existing equipment
located at the Lovelock Lateral Tap. These facilities typically have a small awning structure to protect
electrical equipment, include a permanent access road, and are fenced for security. Locations are listed
above in Table 1.2-4, and land requirements for the sites are located within are listed below in Table 1.2-6.

Mainline Valves and Sideline Valves

MLVs will be installed at intervals not to exceed maximum intervals per class location, as defined in U.S.
Department of Transportation’s (USDOT’s) Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration
(PHMSA) 49 CFR 192.179. MLVs will be located within the permanent rights-of-way along the 48-inch

Launchers/Receivers

Launchers and receivers will be installed at various locations along the Project to allow for system cleaning

fenced for security purposes. Various launcher/receiver facilities will be located along the Project route,
for example at new and existing MLV sites, as listed in Table 1.2-4 above.

Small Distribution Regulator Stations

Small distribution regulator stations (SDRS) provide natural gas regulation at taps for small customer
service lines. There are two SDRS in this Project as listed in Table 1.2-4 above and each is approximately
one-tenth of an acre in size. Springer Mine SDRS and Humboldt House SDRS are near locations on the
16-inch Mainline where Existing Shippers have taps. Two new SDRS will be installed on the 48-inch
Lincoln Lateral to serve these Existing Shippers. These facilities will include a permanent access road and
will be fenced for security purposes.

1.2.2.3    Abandonment of Facilities

Great Basin will abandon existing pipeline and compressor station facilities as noted in Table 1.2-5 and
described in Section 1.2.1, Purpose and Need. These abandoned facilities will no longer be required to
deliver Great Basin’s total contracted firm capacity once the Project is placed in service. The MAOP of
the 16-inch Mainline planned for abandonment is 830 psig; the MAOP of the 8-inch Gabbs Lateral planned
for abandonment is 400 psig. As noted in Section 1.2.1, Great Basin requests that the Commission allow
Great Basin to abandon these facilities in 2030, to allow it to operate its new system and provide service to
all Great Basin Shippers for approximately one year before beginning abandonment of the existing pipelines
and compressor stations.

1.3       Construction Schedule and Workforce

Great Basin assumes that the Commission will issue a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity in
November 2027 and Notice to Proceed Authorization by January 2028. Great Basin also assumes that all
other federal, state, county/local permits, including right-of-way grants, will be obtained no later than
January 2028. Based on these assumptions for authorizations and approvals, Great Basin anticipates that
Project construction will commence late 2027/early 2028 and extend through October 2028, with a
projected in-service date of November 1, 2028.

Great Basin anticipates that the Project will be constructed in four pipeline spreads, which represents a
continuous operation of equipment and crews handling various phases of construction activities. The final
decision regarding the total number of spreads will be determined following Great Basin’s selection of the
Project’s pipeline construction contractor(s). A construction spread typically consists of a pipeline crew
and a crossing crew, as necessary for road and waterbody crossings. Spread breaks of the 48-inch Lincoln
Lateral by MP and Project Laterals are currently planned as follows:

      •    Spread 2 includes LI-50.7 to LI-109.2,

      •    Spread 4 includes LI-160.2 to LI-206.7 and the following Project Laterals:

Great Basin will provide the Commission with an updated and detailed construction schedule, including
sequencing of construction by spread, upon Great Basin’s selection of the pipeline construction
contractor(s). The currently proposed workforce is included in Resource Report 5.

Project construction will typically be conducted seven days a week between the hours of 7 a.m. and 7 p.m.
Weather conditions, site conditions, specialized construction techniques including HDDs, hydrostatic
testing, emergencies, stream crossing timing windows, and blasting may necessitate nighttime (after 7 p.m.)
extended work hours, including 24-hour operation or no work stoppage, and/or extended work on holidays.
Tie-in activities (including pressure reductions, venting, tapping, and plugging), other testing and

hours with little disruption to the surrounding environment and public. Nighttime work, 24-hour operation,
and extended work on holidays, is currently anticipated to be needed for activities requiring continuity of
work, for example HDD drilling and electric instrumentation and controls work at the Jungo Compressor

1.4   Contractor Evaluation

Great Basin will perform an extensive, in-depth evaluation of potential pipeline construction contractors
which will include the selection of one or more specialized pipeline construction contractor(s) through a
competitive bid process. This process ensures that the Project will be constructed by a reputable
contractor(s) with expertise in large diameter steel projects. The screening process of potential contractors
will include the review of the contractor’s financial statements, reports of Occupational Safety and Health
Administration commendations and violations, training and safety programs, current contractor and
business licenses, total amount of commitments under contract, review of recently completed projects for
other companies, proof of insurance, experience and performance on interstate natural gas transmission-
related projects, and the availability and condition of fleet and excavation equipment. Great Basin will also
perform a series of interviews and check the references provided. Great Basin will evaluate all the
information gathered and observed to determine if the pipeline construction contractor(s) will be placed on
the approved bidder list for this Project.

Great Basin plans to issue a bid invitation to all approved pipeline construction contractors. Great Basin’s
approved bidder list will include pipeline construction contractors that are both union and non-union. The
successful pipeline construction contractor(s) will be responsible for employing the workers needed to
construct the pipeline to the standards incorporated into the contract. Great Basin assumes local businesses
will supply temporary housing to support non-local construction workers. No other additional temporary
housing needs are expected to facilitate Project construction. If housing is deemed insufficient, a worker
camp (i.e., workspace for non-local workers to live in trailers during construction) will be proposed. Local
workers may be hired by the pipeline construction contractor(s), a subcontractor, or by a local company
providing materials, supplies, or services to the contractor(s).

Great Basin and its appointed engineering, procurement and construction management consultant (TRC)
will manage and supervise the pipeline construction contractor(s). Great Basin will oversee and inspect all
contractor work based on federally mandated minimum standards, applicable permit requirements, and
Great Basin’s internal policies and procedures.

1.5.1     Standard Construction and Restoration Procedures

Standard construction procedures to install the 48-inch Lincoln Lateral and Project Laterals include rights-
of-way/survey staking; vegetation clearing; workspace grading; installation of erosion and sediment control
devices; trench excavation; stringing; pipeline preparation (bending, welding, joint coating [including
inspection and coating repair], lowering-in, and tie-in); backfilling and rough grading; hydrostatic testing;
and cleanup, site restoration, and revegetation. The following sections identify these standard construction
procedures and restoration techniques for routine pipeline construction.

Areas requiring specialized construction procedures, such as residential areas; agricultural areas; road,
railroad, and utility crossings; trenchless construction methods such as boring and HDD; areas requiring
blasting/rock removal; waterbody and wetland crossings; crossings of unusual topographies such as
unstable soils and trench conditions, steep slopes, or side slopes; and areas with environmentally restricted

Prior to the start of construction, land surveyors will demarcate each pipeline centerline, all points of
intersection, the boundaries of the construction workspace on both private and public lands, and all TWS
with stakes and/or flagging. The pipeline construction contractor(s) will be responsible for maintaining the
staking and reference of the rights-of-way and will also ensure that all construction disturbance remains
within the Project’s right-of-way. The pipeline construction contractor(s) will “Call Before You Dig” or
“811” to verify, stake, and flag buried utilities within the rights-of-way to prevent any damage. Sensitive
biological and cultural resources identified by federal, state, and local agencies or landowner easement
agreements will be located, staked, and flagged by the pipeline construction contractor(s) prior to
construction to prevent accidental damage during pipeline construction.

permanent disturbance footprints, to provide safe and efficient work areas for all phases of pipeline

mechanical or hand cutting techniques. Herbaceous vegetation will be mowed to ground level. No cleared
material will be placed in a waterbody or wetland.

Tree clearing, if needed, will be conducted in accordance with the requirements of the Migratory Bird
Treaty Act, permit conditions, and agency-directed conservation plans. Cleared trees may be chipped on

1.5.1.3   Trenching

A trench will be excavated to the appropriate depth to allow for the burial of the pipe with a minimum of
36 inches of cover, as required for natural gas transmission pipelines by USDOT regulations (49 CFR Part
192). In uplands, the trench will be dug with a track-mounted excavator or crawler-mounted
ditching/trenching machine, and the excavated material will be placed next to the trench (nonworking side)
within the limits of the construction right-of-way. In wetlands and waterbodies, an excavator will be used.
When stockpiled, subsoils will be segregated from topsoil during trenching to minimize impacts on the soil
profile. If it becomes necessary to remove water from the trench, water will be pumped to a well-vegetated
upland area (where practicable) off the right-of-way and filtered through a filter bag or siltation barrier.

In upland areas, the trench will be excavated to ensure compliance with USDOT cover requirements by
achieving sufficient burial depth for the pipeline. The trench generally will be at least 24 inches wider than
the diameter of the pipe. Site-specific conditions, such as unconsolidated soils, may warrant a greater trench
width or depth, which will be determined during detailed engineering and construction.

1.5.1.4   Stringing

Stringing involves moving the pipe segments into position along the right-of-way in preparation for the
bending, welding, and laying operations. The pipe joints will be lined up end-to-end to allow for welding
into continuous lengths of pipe known as strings. Stringing activities will be coordinated with the trenching
and pipe-laying crews to minimize potential impacts on traffic, livestock, or wildlife across the rights-of-
way. Pipe segments will be laid to avoid damage to erosion and sediment control devices.

1.5.1.5   Bending

Bending of the pipe is required to allow the pipeline to follow the natural grade and directional changes of
the rights-of-way. This operation utilizes a bending engineer who will measure the angles and tangents of
the trench to calculate the bend degree and orientation necessary for each pipe length. Selected joints will
be field-bent by a track-mounted hydraulic bending machine. Manufactured bends will be used for larger
horizontal and vertical changes of direction.

1.5.1.6   Welding

Following stringing and bending, the joints of pipe will be placed on cribbing supports adjacent to the
trench. The ends will be carefully aligned and welded together using multiple passes for a full penetration
weld. All welding will be performed in accordance with the American Petroleum Institute (API) Standard
No. 1104. Individual pipe segments will be welded in either one or two steps. Welding will be performed
in a single step if automated welding is utilized by the construction contractor(s). If manual welding is
performed, the front-end welding crew will complete the stringer beads and the hot pass, and the back-end
welding crew will complete the filler beads and cap.

To ensure weld quality and integrity, all welds will be non-destructively examined (e.g., radiography [x-
ray] and/or magnetic particle test) in accordance with USDOT regulations Title 49 CFR Part 192. Any
welds displaying unacceptable defects will be repaired or removed and new welds will be installed and re-
examined. The pipeline construction contractor(s) will take all precautionary measures to reduce the chance
of igniting a fire during welding and grinding operations. These precautions include the use of a fire watch
and placing a fire-resistant mat on the ground below welding and grinding operations whenever dry
vegetation is present.

1.5.1.7   Joint Coating

After welds have been non-destructively examined and approved, the weld areas (or joints) will be coated
by a coating crew. The pipe coating will be inspected for quality and integrity using equipment that emits
an electrical charge. The pipeline coating will be electrically insulated, and the electrical charge will detect
any gaps in the coating. This external pipeline and joint coating, along with the cathodic protection system,
will protect the steel pipe from corrosion. The pipeline coating, except for a small area at the end of the
pipe joint, is applied at the pipe mill or coating yard before shipment to the Project site.

1.5.1.8   Lowering-In and Tie-Ins

After welding, non-destructive examination, joint coating, and inspecting, the trench will be cleared of any
debris, and any water will be pumped out of the trench into a well-vegetated upland area through an
approved filter bag. The pipe strings will then be lowered into the trench using side boom tractors.

Once the pipe strings have been lowered in, a tie-in crew will make the final welds in the trench. The ends
of each pipe string will be welded together, non-destructively examined, and coated.

1.5.1.9   Backfilling

After the pipe is installed, excavated spoil material will be used to cover the pipe using techniques to protect
the pipe and coating from damage. All suitable material (loose earthen materials free of rocks and hard
chunks) excavated from the trench will be replaced during backfilling (first with subsoil, then spreading
topsoil over the top). In areas where excavated material is unsuitable for backfilling, additional fill may be
imported from off-site. The top of the trench may be slightly crowned, except in wetlands, to compensate
for potential settling. The surface will be compacted and scarified, as necessary.

In rocky areas, padding material (i.e., original trench spoils screened of rock or imported, rock-free fill
material) will be used to cover and protect the pipeline and coating from rocks. The remaining trench spoils
will be backfilled after padding is completed. After the trench is filled to ground level, the backfill will be
compacted.

Topsoil will not be used for padding or backfill. Topsoil and subsoil (including trench spoils) will remain
segregated during backfilling. Vegetation or other debris will not be mixed with topsoil or subsoil.
Equipment and vehicles will not be allowed to drive over topsoil or subsoil piles during construction.

1.5.1.10 Cleaning

Debris will be removed from all construction work areas, unless leaving materials onsite for beneficial
reuse, stabilization, and/or habitat restoration is approved by the landowner and/or land managing agency.
Materials unsuitable for use as backfill and economically not usable for other purposes will be disposed of
in available landfills in accordance with local and county guidelines. Disposal will be in accordance with
applicable local, state, or federal laws, rules, and regulations.

Following the completion of the pipeline tie-ins, the pipeline will be internally cleaned with pigs. A
manifold will be installed on one end of a long pipeline section, and pigs will be propelled by compressed
air through the pipeline and into an open pig catcher. The pigs will remove any dirt, water, or debris that
inadvertently collect within the pipeline during the construction process.

1.5.1.11 Hydrostatic Testing

Following cleaning, the pipeline will be pressure tested to ensure its integrity for the intended service and
operating pressure. Water will be used to hydrostatically test the pipeline. Hydrostatic test water will be
obtained from available municipal sources and/or known sources. The water will be pumped from the water
source into the pipeline and will propel a pig through the pipeline in a manner that fills the pipeline with
water. A high-pressure pump will be used to add water to the test section and to increase the test pressure.
At the completion of the hydrostatic test, the pressure will be removed from the test section by propelling
the pig with air and dewatering the pipe. Water will be tested for pollutants in accordance with permitting
requirements prior to discharge. Additional drying pig runs will be made, as necessary, to remove any
residual water from the pipeline. Hydrostatic testing requirements, water sources, and discharge locations
are provided in Resource Report 2 and detailed in the Project’s Hydrostatic Test Plan (Appendix 1.D-5)

1.5.1.12 Restoration of Topography

A cleanup crew will complete the restoration of the right-of-way and temporary construction workspaces.
Weather and soil conditions permitting, final cleanup and installation of permanent erosion control
measures for each identified construction spread will be completed within ten days after the trench is
backfilled. All graded areas will be restored to as near the natural or preexisting grade as practicable. Steep
cuts will be restored to a stable position and protected by appropriate erosion control measures in areas of
erosive soils or slopes with potential for slumping or landslides. Steep slopes are further discussed in
Resource Report 6.

Additional areas requiring further restoration activities may be identified during construction. Excess spoils
will be removed from the right-of-way and disposed of in accordance with applicable laws, rules, and
regulations (including the Project Plan for beneficial reuse) in an area deemed appropriate by the landowner
and land management agency. Excess spoils will not be placed in wetland areas. In upland areas, a center
berm or crown approximately 8 inches high may be left over the trench line to allow for additional settling.

Once recontouring is complete, subsoil compaction will be conducted in all disturbance areas by ripping,
discing, or chisel plowing, unless otherwise directed by the landowner and/or land management agency.
This procedure will be completed before topsoil is replaced atop the disturbed surface, except where thin
topsoil overlays rocky subsoil. Before topsoil is replaced, excess rock on the surface will be removed and
disposed of in accordance with applicable laws, rules, and regulations (including the Project Plan for
beneficial reuse) in an area deemed appropriate by the landowner and/or land management agency.

Topsoil will be replaced over restored areas of the construction right-of-way. If necessary, topsoil
decompaction may be performed by ripping, discing, or chisel plowing. Discing and tilling will be
completed parallel to all slope contours. To minimize water and wind erosion and provide a seed bed for
revegetation, topsoil will be left in a roughened condition.

Permanent slope breakers will be constructed to stabilize upstream or upslope areas and to divert surface
water away from the backfilled trench and into stable, well-vegetated areas. These measures will prevent
channeling along the trench line on hillsides or sloped landscapes. Trench breakers will be installed in
conjunction with slope breakers to prevent water from preferentially flowing along the backfilled trench.
Tackifiers will be applied on the surface of steep slopes or uneven terrain to minimize sediment loss. Rock
will be replaced on the surface in areas where exposed bedrock is present. Rock replacement will match
the undisturbed areas adjacent to the right-of-way, to the extent practicable. Temporary erosion control
devices will be removed when replaced by permanent erosion control devices.

1.5.1.13 Revegetation

Revegetation is the final phase of pipeline construction, shifting the focus towards environmental
stewardship. The primary objective of revegetation hinges on the permanent reestablishment of native
vegetation (plant) cover to control erosion and sedimentation and restore biological habitats. The
reestablishment of vegetation will also reduce the visual impacts of the pipeline corridor. A vegetative
cover composed of compatible native species, similar in composition to pre-construction conditions, will
be re-established on non-agricultural lands. Revegetation will be accomplished by following the Project
Plan (Appendix 1.D-1) and the Restoration and Revegetation Plan (Appendix 1.D-10), and approved by
landowners and/or land management agencies.

Erosion control materials, such as mulching and tackifier application aid in the retention of soil moisture
and minimize topsoil erosion by wind and water. Mulching or tackifiers may be utilized in areas of extreme
exposure to wind, unstable slopes, or highly erodible soils. Weed-free straw will be used as mulch or as
directed by the landowner and/or land management agency. Mulch will be anchored to the ground using a
crimper or disc. On steep slopes, an erosion control blanket may be used in lieu of mulch.

Post-construction revegetation monitoring, reporting, and ongoing maintenance will be performed in
accordance with the Project Plan (Appendix 1.D-1) and approved by landowner and/or land management
agency reclamation requirements.

1.5.2.4   Trenchless Construction Methods

Trenchless construction techniques, such as boring and HDD technologies, may be used to construct
pipelines to minimize impacts on resources such as waterbodies, wetlands, roadways, and sensitive areas.
With these methods, the pipeline is installed below the resource using equipment staged at the resources’
boundary.

Boring

Auger boring (also known as jack and bore) is a trenchless construction method used for shorter and
straighter crossings. Auger boring consists of creating a shaft for a pipe to be installed by means of a
conventional auger, pneumatic hammering, hydraulic ramming, guided bore set-ups, tunnelling, micro-
tunnelling, telescoping, and other such methods. The boring technique is accomplished by first excavating
a bore pit and a receiving pit. The bore pit is excavated to a depth slightly deeper than the planned
installation depth of the pipe and is graded such that the bore will follow the anticipated installation angle.
A boring machine is then lowered to the bottom of the bore pit to install the pipe. A machine with a cutting
head is used to cut the soil as it progresses underneath the feature being crossed, the soils are removed, and
a void is created in which the pipe is installed.

Great Basin will work with the pipeline construction contractor(s) and specialized subcontractor (if
applicable) during construction to ensure that the proper equipment is utilized per the approved permits and
onsite conditions prior to installation. After installation, the bored pipeline segment is welded to the
adjacent pipeline segments at the entry and exit. The needed workspace configuration for boring operations,
including boring machine setup, cuttings/return settlement and storage pits, pipe storage, entry and exit pit
spoil storage, and construction equipment staging necessary to support the operation varies depending on
length of the bore, the terrain, and layout at each site. Typical boring workspace configurations, and actual
staging dimensions are provided in Appendix 1.F (Typical Construction Drawings and Details).

The major factors limiting the success of a boring operation include subsurface soil, geologic conditions,
and the presence of groundwater; bore length, diameter, and alignment constraints; equipment and method
selection; and drilling fluid and spoil management. Topography at a site may also limit the use of this
method; preferred locations are generally level or have moderately convex terrain, such that the depth of
the bore pit does not present concerns relative to constructability or safety. Subsurface soil, geologic, and
groundwater conditions must be conducive to establishing and maintaining safe bore and receiving pit
excavations and allow the equipment to conduct a successful bore. Boring operations typically occur over
a crossing distance of 40 to 500 feet, depending on the equipment, soils, and setup. Great Basin will work

with the pipeline construction contractor(s) and specialized subcontractor(s) (if applicable) during
construction to ensure that the proper equipment and most appropriate trenchless method is selected to meet
each crossing objective. Drilling fluid, usually bentonite clay, is designed to stabilize the borehole, carry
the cuttings (spoil) from the borehole, cool and lubricate the drill, control groundwater inflow, reduce torque
and backflow, and prevent bore collapse and settlement.

Horizontal Directional Drilling (HDD)

HDD is a trenchless construction method that avoids or minimizes impact on the ground surface by drilling
a hole and pulling the pipeline through it rather than using a trench. The HDD method drills a small-
diameter hole, or pilot hole, and the drill bit is steered and monitored along a predetermined design path
that begins and ends on the surface. Once the pilot hole is complete, the hole is enlarged sufficiently to
accommodate the pipeline to be installed. The pipeline may or may not be installed concurrently with the
hole enlargement, depending on the final diameter of the enlarged hole and the soil conditions encountered.
During this process, drilling fluid, normally consisting of bentonite clay and water from an approved source,
will be circulated through the hole to power and lubricate the cutting bit, remove cuttings to the surface,
and maintain the integrity of the hole. Workspaces are located on either end of the HDD typically require
a 250-foot by 250-foot area but may require more if the pipeline changes direction near the start or end of
the drill. HDD work also requires a temporary HDD pullback area to layout the welded pipe segment that
will be pulled through the drill. If the HDD pullback area is aligned with the construction workspace, then
no additional pullback area is needed; however, if the pullback is not aligned with construction workspace,
a pullback space that is typically fifty-feet-wide and as long as the welded pipe segment that will be pulled
through is needed.

Great Basin’s Project HDD Procedures and Mud Monitoring Plan (HDD Plan) (Appendix 1.D-4), describes
procedures to be used to monitor, contain, and clean any inadvertent releases of drilling fluid. The HDD

Special construction techniques may be employed where the slope gradient exceeds 15 percent, where
construction activity must be conducted on side slopes, or where ground conditions warrant the use of such
techniques to ensure the safety of workers, the public, or the environment. Pipe installation and construction
activities across steep or side slopes will be similar to standard upland construction methods; however,
equipment may be tethered via a winch line to other stabilized equipment at the top of the slope.

Various heavy equipment used for construction may be outfitted with winches and cables with sufficient
capacity to support the weight of active heavy equipment working on the slope and/or materials. This
technique provides a simple arrest to uncontrolled movements and can function as an assist to equipment
when traversing across or up and down the slope within the right-of-way. In this manner, equipment used
to prepare the construction corridor and excavate the trench will be secured with a series of winch tractors
to maintain control and provide an additional level of safety. All necessary and appropriate equipment and
attachment point inspections will be conducted prior to daily operation by the pipeline construction
contractor(s), or more frequently if deemed necessary, as a best management practice. Spoil piles adjacent
to the trench will be stabilized with temporary erosion control devices to keep excavated soil within the
construction work area. All erosion control devices will be installed in accordance with the Project Plan
and Procedures (with requested alternative measures provided in the Project Plan and Procedures
documents Appendix 1.D).

In areas where pipeline construction involves side slopes, cut and fill grading may be necessary to create a
safe, flat work terrace. Soil from the construction work area will be excavated and moved to be stockpiled
as spoil or to create a temporary fill to support activity. After the pipeline is installed, the slope’s original
contours will be restored to the extent practicable. Resource Report 6, Table 6.A.3 includes information
on slope along the Project. Great Basin continues to evaluate slopes over 15 percent to assess whether
original contours will be restored, or if another restoration method will be used. Once this information has
been finalized, Great Basin will update this Section 1.5.2.7, Section 1.5.1.2, and Resource Report 6
accordingly with the Application Filing.

Grading may be minimized by detouring non-essential equipment around areas of excessively steep slopes
using an approved temporary access road or bypass. Two-toning (i.e., grading two small cuts where the
working side is higher than the spoil side) may also be implemented to minimize grading for steep slopes.

The Project will install temporary trench plugs and temporary slope breakers during construction on slopes
in accordance with the Project Plan. Temporary slope breakers will channel water off the right-of-way into
a well-vegetated area or into an energy dissipating device at the end of the breaker. Temporary trench plugs
will reduce the velocity of water flowing along the trench and the volume of water that collects at the bottom
of slopes. Permanent trench breakers and permanent slope breakers will be installed on steep slopes.
Trench breakers are designed to prevent preferential water flow along the pipeline trench by diverting
subsurface water flow to the land surface. Groundwater discharging to the land surface will then be
redirected off the right-of-way by slope breakers. When used in combination, these structures prevent
subsurface piping of soils, which can lead to slope instability and failure.

1.5.2.9    Abandonment of Pipe (In place)

As stated in Section 1.2.1, approximately 124 miles of existing 16-inch Mainline (installed in 1963) and
approximately 10 miles of existing 8-inch Gabbs Lateral (installed in 1964) will be abandoned in place.
These abandoned facilities will no longer be required to deliver Great Basin’s total contracted firm capacity
once the Project is placed into service. Great Basin anticipates that these existing pipelines will be
abandoned in place, except for small segments of pipeline to be removed at each cut and cap location and
areas that could be exposed by future erosion. Great Basin will notify landowners of its proposed method
of abandonment in place in the landowner notification letter sent when the Application is filed 8. If requested
by the landowner, Great Basin will discuss Great Basin’s preferred method and other options such as
abandonment by removal. Great Basin will abandon the pipeline using the method approved by the
landowner. Great Basin will retain the pipeline easement for the segments of the 16-inch Mainline and 8-
inch Gabbs Lateral and be responsible for facilities that are abandoned in place.

To facilitate this abandonment, the pressure in the existing pipelines will be reduced to approximately
5 psig. Once the desired pressure is reached, the remaining natural gas will be vented into the atmosphere.
The pipelines will then be purged with a slug of nitrogen or air. Following the venting and purging, the
existing pipelines will be abandoned in place, disconnected at the take-off (upstream) and terminus
(downstream) tie-in locations, and cut and capped at a specified frequency, generally at approximate five-
mile increments. Waterbody and road crossings identified will be abandoned according to permitting
jurisdiction requirements. A table of locations where flowable fill will be used is provided in Table 1.A-8
in Appendix 1.A.

The dimensions of excavation points required to perform the cuts and caps for abandonment in place are
typically 50 feet by 75 feet. Site conditions at some disconnect locations, such as areas with unstable soils
or other underground utilities, may require excavating a larger and/or deeper trench to ensure safe working
conditions. Excavated materials will be stockpiled within the approved work area. Where topsoil is
stripped, subsoil will be stored separately from topsoil.

After the pipe is exposed at each disconnect location, a small section (approximately 3 to 5 feet) of pipe
will be cut out, removed, and capped by welding steel plates onto both ends of the abandoned pipe
remaining in place. Secondary containment will be placed below the pipe at each cut to capture unexpected
liquids that may be present within the pipe. Liquids captured in secondary containment will be disposed of
properly. After the pipe has been capped, the trench will be backfilled. Previously excavated materials
(including subsoil and topsoil, if applicable) will be redeposited back into the trench using bladed
equipment or backhoes. Subsoil will be used for backfilling and padding, and topsoil will be layered atop
the subsoil. A center crown approximately 8 inches high may be left over the trench line to allow for
potential soil settling. Topsoil compaction will be performed by ripping, discing, or chisel plowing to
minimize trench settling.

In areas that could experience erosion after a rain event, a larger section of pipe (approximately 20 to 30
feet) will be cut out and removed. All other processes and procedures will remain the same as described
above.

The existing pipelines will be disconnected from the cathodic protection equipment. All aboveground
appurtenances, including pipeline markers, valve settings, cathodic protection equipment, pig launchers and
receivers, pipe settings, and other miscellaneous aboveground piping, will be demolished and removed.

    •   Knock the wrap off the pipe using a brass hammer.
    •   Place the wrap and plastic sheet in the 6-mil polyethylene asbestos disposal bag along with
        coveralls, boot covers, and gloves.
    •   Wet the contents inside the disposal bag with the Penewet solution to ensure the fibers do not

    •   Seal the asbestos disposable bag with duct tape.

1.5.4   Belowground Facility Construction - Cathodic Protection

An impressed current cathodic protection (ICCP) system will be installed as part of this Project to help
prevent corrosion and protect the Project pipelines and associated facilities. This ICCP system shall consist
of alternating current (AC) and/or direct current (DC) powered rectifiers and anode ground beds. Deep
well type anode beds, typically installed in vertically drilled holes at approximate depths of 300 to 400 feet
below grade, are preferred. A distributed/surface anode ground bed will be an option that Great Basin may
utilize in the event of ultrahigh soil resistivity at a deep well. Insulated flange gasket kits will be installed
to electrically isolate the pipeline from electronic equipment at locations such as compressor stations,
Delivery Points, and other facilities and appurtenances, which will have their own independent cathodic
protection unit, as necessary. AC powered rectifiers with deep well type anode beds may be installed within
the boundaries of facility sites to facilitate and minimize the efforts of right-of-way acquisition.

Cathodic protection test stations (with and without AC/DC coupon) will be installed at locations specified
on the construction alignment sheets provided with the Application Filing and will be conveniently located
for monitoring and shall be spaced approximately every mile not to exceed 1.5 miles if an impressed current
system, or every ½ mile not to exceed 1 mile for galvanic anode systems.

Great Basin will plan to have these systems installed and in service within three months of the pipeline
being placed into service, but no later than one year from this date. These systems can be constructed up
to one year after the pipeline is placed into service, per USDOT requirements in 49 CFR Part 192.

1.11 Cumulative Impacts

Cumulative impacts may occur from the combined, incremental direct and indirect impacts of an action in
combination with past, present, and reasonably foreseeable future actions (RFFAs) on the environment.
Great Basin will evaluate the potential cumulative effects of the Project on individual resources in
combination with ongoing past and present actions, as well as RFFAs.

Cumulative impacts on a specific resource can occur when the impacts of the Project overlap in space and
time with impacts of other significant planned projects, so long as these impacts take place within the same
general period of time and occur within the specific resource’s cumulative impacts assessment area (CIAA)
associated with the Project.

1.11.1 Cumulative Impacts Assessment Area

The geographic scope for evaluating cumulative impacts on a specific resource is referred to as the CIAA.
The CIAA may differ for each resource depending on a variety of factors, such as a resource’s spatial
distribution or configuration, sensitivity to disturbance, behavior, or administrative boundaries. The CIAAs
used to assess the cumulative impacts of the Project for each type of resource are shown in Table 1.11-1
and depicted in Appendix 1.B-6 (Cumulative Impact Assessment Area Map).

1.11.2 Cumulative Actions

Projects to be considered in the cumulative impact analysis were identified within the CIAAs and include
those projects that would also be expected to impact the same resources as the Project. The furthest extent
of the CIAAs was generally within the counties and other resource management areas encompassed by the
Project components. Past, present, and RFFAs potentially impacting air resources were identified within a
30-mile radius of the proposed new compressor station.

A comprehensive online search of federal, state, and local government websites was conducted to identify
these projects, including websites of the U.S. Department of Interior, Bureau of Land Management; Nevada
Department of Transportation; and Churchill, Humboldt, Lyon, Pershing, Storey, and Washoe counties;
and media outlets. Further sources of project information were obtained through searches of types of
projects with potentially broad geographic scope overlapping the CIAAs and potentially impacting the same
resources as the Project, including new mine and mine expansion projects, transmission line
construction/upgrades, pipeline construction/replacement, and solar projects.

Present projects and RFFAs include projects that were identified in various stages of federal, state and local
agency approval, permitting, and/or construction and that have been sufficiently defined in terms of
geographic area and timeframe to determine the potential for cumulative impacts to occur during the
construction and operation periods of the Project. For purposes of this analysis, projects were selected in
the timeframe between 2025 and 2030. Past projects include those past actions located within the
geographic area of the CIAAs, and that continue to contribute discernable impacts, such as ongoing air or
other emissions or discharges. However, as stated in the FERC Guidance Manual, past actions may also
be considered to “have become part of the existing nature of an area,” and may be considered “part of the
baseline for examining cumulative impacts.”

Table 1.A-11 in Appendix 1.A identifies each of the projects to be considered in the cumulative impact
analysis, and includes information on the type of project, location and approximate size (i.e., acreage,
distance), project sponsor/proponent, and status/schedule as provided in the source material on the project.
Also included in Table 1.A-11 for each project is the estimated distance of the project to the nearest Project
component. and the resources potentially impacted that will be considered in the cumulative impact
analysis. Figure 1.B-6 (Appendix 1.B) shows the location of each of the projects in relation to the Project
components, and boundaries of specific resource CIAAs. References and sources for information on each
project are also shown in Appendix 1.A, Table 1.A-11.

1.11.3 Cumulative Impact Analysis

The cumulative impact analysis will evaluate the cumulative impacts of the Project when combined with
the impacts of past, present and RFFAs occurring within the same timeframe of the Project and the same
geographic area, or CIAA, for each resource.

Each resource report will present the existing environment, including past actions that may be considered
“part of the baseline for examining cumulative impacts,” and impacts of the Project. Impacts will be
characterized as direct or indirect, long- or short-term and whether the impacts are minor, moderate or
potentially significant. Measures to mitigate these impacts also will be discussed.

For those resources impacted by the Project, the cumulative impact analysis will then consider the impacts
of other projects identified in Appendix 1.A, Table 1.A-11, whether those impacts overlap geographically
and temporally within the CIAA, and whether they may result in an additive impact on the same resources

           GREAT BASIN UPLAND EROSION CONTROL, REVEGETATION, AND MAINTENANCE PLAN



I.    APPLICABILITY

      Great Basin Gas Transmission Company (Great Basin) has prepared this 2028 Expansion
      Project (Project) Great Basin Upland Erosion Control, Revegetation, and Maintenance Plan
      (Project Plan) to meet or exceed the best management practices (BMPs) and mitigation
      measures included in the Federal Energy Regulation Commission’s (FERC or
      Commission) Upland Erosion Control, Revegetation and Maintenance Plan (FERC Plan).
      The intent of the Project Plan is to identify baseline mitigation measures for minimizing
      erosion and enhancing revegetation.

      Where the Project Plan departs substantially from the FERC Plan, the Project specific text
      is highlighted by bold text. Other changes throughout the Project Plan are noted in italics.
      Very minor formatting changes (Project sponsor to Great Basin, should to will, etc.) are not
      specifically called out in the Project Plan text. A table showing the major changes from the
      FERC Plan is included in Appendix A of this document.

III.   PRECONSTRUCTION PLANNING

       Great Basin shall do the following before construction:

       A.      CONSTRUCTION WORK AREAS

               1.     Identify all construction work areas (e.g., construction right-of-way, extra
                      work space areas, pipe storage and contractor yards, borrow and disposal
                      areas, access roads) that would be needed for safe construction. Great Basin
                      will ensure that appropriate cultural resources and biological surveys are
                      conducted, as determined necessary by the appropriate federal and state
                      agencies.

               2.     Great Basin has expanded cultural resources and endangered species
                      surveys to include buffers beyond authorized work areas.

               3.     Plan construction sequencing to limit the amount and duration of open trench
                      sections, as necessary, to prevent excessive erosion or sediment flow into
                      sensitive environmental resource areas.

       B.      GRAZING DEFERMENT

               Develop grazing deferment plans with willing landowners, grazing permittees,
               and land management agencies to minimize grazing disturbance of revegetation
               efforts.

       C.      ROAD CROSSINGS AND ACCESS POINTS

               Plan for safe and accessible conditions at all roadway crossings and access points
               during construction and restoration.

       D.      DISPOSAL PLANNING

               Determine methods and locations for the regular collection, containment, and
               disposal of excess construction materials and debris (e.g., timber, slash, mats,
               garbage, drill cuttings and fluids, excess rock) throughout the construction process.
               Off-site disposal in other than commercially operated disposal locations is
               subject to compliance with all applicable survey, landowner permission, and
               mitigation requirements. Disposal of materials for beneficial reuse must not result
               in adverse environmental impact and is subject to compliance with all applicable
               survey, landowner or land management agency approval, and permit requirements.

B.      TOPSOIL SEGREGATION

        1.     Unless the landowner or land management agency specifically approves
               otherwise, prevent the mixing of topsoil with subsoil by stripping topsoil
               from either the full work area or from the trench and subsoil storage area
               (ditch plus spoil side method) in:

               a.     cultivated or rotated croplands, and managed pastures;

               b.     residential areas;

               c.     hayfields; and

               d.     other areas at the landowner’s or land managing agency’s request.

        2.     In residential areas, importation of topsoil is an acceptable alternative to
               topsoil segregation.

        3.     Where topsoil segregation is required, Great Basin must:

               a.     segregate at least 12 inches of topsoil in deep soils (more than 12
                      inches of topsoil); and

               b.     make every effort to segregate the entire topsoil layer in soils with
                      less than 12 inches of topsoil.

        4.     Maintain separation of salvaged topsoil and subsoil throughout all
               construction activities.

        5.     Segregated topsoil may not be used for padding the pipe, constructing
               temporary slope breakers or trench plugs, improving or maintaining roads,
               or as a fill material.

        6.     Stabilize topsoil piles and minimize loss due to wind and water erosion with
               use of sediment barriers, mulch, temporary seeding, tackifiers, or functional
               equivalents, where necessary.

   2.     Temporary Trench Plugs

          Temporary trench plugs are intended to segment a continuous open trench
          prior to backfill.

          a.      Temporary trench plugs may consist of unexcavated portions of

                  equivalent.

          b.      Position temporary trench plugs, as necessary, to reduce trenchline

                  at the base of slopes.

   3.     Sediment Barriers

          Sediment barriers are intended to stop the flow of sediments and to prevent
          the deposition of sediments beyond approved workspaces or into sensitive
          resources.

          a.      Sediment barriers may be constructed of materials such as silt fence,
                  staked hay or straw bales, compacted earth (e.g., driveable berms
                  across travelways), sand bags, or other appropriate materials.

          b.      At a minimum, install and maintain temporary sediment barriers
                  across the entire construction right-of-way at the base of slopes
                  greater than 5 percent where the base of the slope is less than 50 feet
                  from a waterbody, wetland, or road crossing until revegetation is
                  successful as defined in this Plan. Leave adequate room between the
                  base of the slope and the sediment barrier to accommodate ponding
                  of water and sediment deposition.

          c.      Where wetlands or waterbodies are adjacent to and downslope of
                  construction work areas, install sediment barriers along the edge of
                  these areas, as necessary to prevent sediment flow into the wetland
                  or waterbody.

   4.     Mulch

          a.      Apply mulch on all slopes (except in cultivated cropland)
                  concurrent with or immediately after seeding, where necessary to
                  stabilize the soil surface and to reduce wind and water erosion.
                  Spread mulch uniformly over the area to cover at least 75 percent
                  of the ground surface at a rate of 2 tons/acre of straw or its
                  equivalent, unless the local soil conservation authority, landowner,
                  or land managing agency approves otherwise in writing.

B.      PERMANENT EROSION CONTROL DEVICES

                     trench breakers.

                     need for and spacing of trench breakers. Otherwise, trench
                     breakers shall be installed at the same spacing as and upslope of
                     permanent slope breakers.

               c.    In agricultural fields and residential areas where slope breakers are
                     not typically required, install trench breakers at the same spacing
                     as if permanent slope breakers were required.

               d.    At a minimum, install a trench breaker at the base of slopes greater
                     than 5 percent where the base of the slope is less than 50 feet from a
                     waterbody or wetland and where needed to avoid draining a
                     waterbody or wetland. Install trench breakers at wetland
                     boundaries, as specified in the Procedures. Do not install trench
                     breakers within a wetland.

              1.     Conduct follow-up inspections of all disturbed areas, as necessary, to

                     a minimum, conduct inspections after the first and second growing seasons.

              2.     Revegetation shall be considered successful if upon visual survey the
                     density and cover of non-nuisance vegetation are similar in density and
                     cover to adjacent undisturbed lands.

                     Continue revegetation efforts until revegetation is successful.

              3.     Monitor and correct problems with drainage and irrigation systems resulting
                     from pipeline construction in agricultural areas until restoration is
                     successful.

              4.     Restoration shall be considered successful if the right-of-way surface
                     condition is similar to adjacent undisturbed lands, construction debris is
                     removed (unless otherwise approved by the landowner or land managing
                     agency per section V.A.6), revegetation is successful, and proper drainage
                     has been restored.

                     right-of-way in uplands shall not be done more frequently than every 3
                     years. However, to facilitate periodic corrosion/leak surveys, a corridor not
                     exceeding 10 feet in width centered on the pipeline may be cleared at a
                     frequency necessary to maintain the 10-foot corridor in an herbaceous state.

I.     APPLICABILITY

       A.        Great Basin Gas Transmission Company (Great Basin) has prepared this 2028
                 Expansion Project (Project) Great Basin Wetland and Waterbody Construction and
                 Mitigation Procedures (Project Procedures) to meet or exceed the best management
                 practices and mitigation measures included in the Federal Energy Regulation
                 Commission’s (FERC or Commission) Wetland and Waterbody Construction and
                 Mitigation Procedures (FERC Procedures). The intent of the Project Procedures is
                 to identify baseline mitigation measures for minimizing the extent and duration of
                 project-related disturbance on wetlands and waterbodies.

                 Where the Project Procedures departs substantially from the FERC Procedures, the
                 Project specific text is highlighted by bold text. Other changes throughout the
                 Project Procedures are noted in italics. Very minor formatting changes (Project
                 sponsor to Great Basin, should to will, etc.) are not specifically called out in the
                 Great Basin Project Procedures text. A table showing the major changes from the
                 FERC Procedures is included in Attachment A of this document.

                 These Project Procedures only apply to wetlands and waterbody areas of the
                 Project. Project-related impacts on non-wetland areas are addressed in the Great
                 Basin Upland Erosion Control, Revegetation, and Maintenance Plan (Project Plan)
                 in Appendix 1.D-1.

                 Alternative measures that differ from those contained in the Project Procedures will
                 only be permitted as certified by the Commission or by written approval of the
                 Director of the Office of Energy Projects (OEP) or designee.

       B.        DEFINITIONS

                 1.     “Waterbody” includes any natural or artificial stream, river, or drainage
                        with perceptible flow at the time of crossing, and other permanent
                        waterbodies such as ponds and lakes:

                        a.      “minor waterbody” includes all waterbodies less than or equal to 10
                                feet wide at the water’s edge at the time of crossing;

                        b.      “intermediate waterbody” includes all waterbodies greater than 10
                                feet wide but less than or equal to 100 feet wide at the water’s edge
                                at the time of crossing; and

                        c.      “major waterbody” includes all waterbodies greater than 100 feet
                                wide at the water’s edge at the time of crossing.

       D.        POST-CONSTRUCTION MAINTENANCE AND REPORTING

                 1.     Do not conduct routine vegetation mowing or clearing over the full width
                        of the permanent right-of-way in wetlands. However, to facilitate periodic
                        corrosion/leak surveys, a corridor centered on the pipeline and up to 10 feet
                        wide may be cleared at a frequency necessary to maintain the 10-foot
                        corridor in an herbaceous state. In addition, trees within 15 feet of the
                        pipeline with roots that could compromise the integrity of pipeline coating
                        may be selectively cut and removed from the permanent right-of-way. Do
                        not conduct any routine vegetation mowing or clearing in wetlands that are
                        between HDD entry and exit points.

                 2.     Do not use herbicides or pesticides in or within 100 feet of a wetland, except
                        as allowed by the appropriate federal or state agency.

                 3.     Time of year restrictions specified in section VII.A.5 of the Project Plan
                        (April 15 – August 1 of any year) apply to routine mowing and clearing of
                        wetland areas.

                 4.     Monitor and record the success of wetland revegetation annually until

                 5.     Wetland revegetation shall be considered successful if all of the following
                        criteria are satisfied:

                        a.     the affected wetland satisfies the current federal definition for a
                               wetland (i.e., soils, hydrology, and vegetation);

                        b.      vegetation is at least 80 percent of either the cover documented for
                               the wetland prior to construction, or at least 80 percent of the cover
                               in adjacent wetland areas that were not disturbed by construction;

                        c.      if natural rather than active revegetation was used, the plant species
                               composition is consistent with early successional wetland plant
                               communities in the affected ecoregion; and

                        d.     invasive species and noxious weeds are absent, unless they are
                               abundant in adjacent areas that were not disturbed by construction.

                 6.     Within 3 years after construction, file a report with the Secretary identifying
                        the status of the wetland revegetation efforts and documenting success as
                        defined in section VI.D.5, above. The requirement to file wetland
                        restoration reports with the Secretary does not apply to projects constructed
                        under the automatic authorization, prior notice, or advance notice
                        provisions in the FERC’s regulations.

                        For any wetland where revegetation is not successful at the end of 3 years
                        after construction, develop and implement (in consultation with a
                        professional wetland ecologist) a remedial revegetation plan to actively
                        revegetate wetlands. Continue revegetation efforts and file a report annually
                        documenting progress in these wetlands until wetland revegetation is
                        successful. Do not use herbicides or pesticides in or within 100 feet of a
                        wetland, except as allowed by the appropriate federal or state agency.

       B.        GENERAL

                 1.     Perform 100 percent radiographic inspection of all pipeline section welds
                        or hydrotest the pipeline sections, before installation under waterbodies or
                        wetlands.

                 2.     If pumps used for hydrostatic testing are within 100 feet of any waterbody
                        or wetland, address secondary containment and refueling of these pumps in
                        the project’s Spill Prevention and Response Procedures.

                 3.     Great Basin will file with the Secretary before construction a list identifying
                        the location of all waterbodies proposed for use as a hydrostatic test water
                        source or discharge location. This filing requirement does not apply to
                        projects constructed under the automatic authorization provisions of the
                        FERC’s regulations. Great Basin may use municipal and county sources
                        for hydrostatic testing and other construction uses.

       C.        INTAKE SOURCE AND RATE

                 1.     Screen the intake hose to minimize the potential for entrainment of fish.

                 2.     Do not use state-designated exceptional value waters, waterbodies which
                        provide habitat for federally listed threatened or endangered species, or
                        waterbodies designated as public water supplies, unless appropriate federal,
                        state, and/or local permitting agencies grant written permission.

                 3.     Maintain adequate flow rates to protect aquatic life, provide for all
                        waterbody uses, and provide for downstream withdrawals of water by
                        existing users.

                 4.     Locate hydrostatic test manifolds outside wetlands and riparian areas to the
                        maximum extent practicable.

       D.        DISCHARGE LOCATION, METHOD, AND RATE

                 1.     Regulate discharge rate, use energy dissipation device(s), and install
                        sediment barriers, as necessary, to prevent erosion, streambed scour,
                        suspension of sediments, or excessive streamflow.

1.0 Introduction
This Spill Prevention, Control, and Countermeasures Plan (SPCC) Plan was prepared for construction
activities associated with Great Basin Gas Transmission Company’s (Great Basin) 2028 Expansion Project
(Project).

1.1     Objectives of the SPCC Plan

The objectives of the SPCC Plan are to:

      1. Prevent the discharge of oil, oil-based products and other regulated material using good engineering
         practices and management controls into navigable Waters of the United States;

      2. Describe the measures implemented at the Project site to prevent oil discharges from occurring;
         and

      3. Prepare Great Basin to respond in a safe, effective and timely manner to mitigate the impacts of a
         discharge.

1.2     Regulatory Applicability

In accordance with 40 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) 112, all facilities engaged in drilling, producing,
gathering, storing, processing, refining, transferring, distributing, using, or consuming oil and oil-based
products must prepare and implement a SPCC Plan if they meet the following criteria:

      1. The Project is non-transportation-related;

      2. The total aboveground storage capacity of oil (containers with capacities equal to or greater than
         55 gallons and including oil filled operational equipment) is more than 1,320 gallons, or the total
         underground storage capacity of oil is greater than 42,000 gallons; and

      3. The Project, due to its location, could reasonably be expected to discharge oil in quantities that may
         be harmful into or upon the navigable waters of the United States or adjoining shorelines.

The Project stores more than 1,320 gallons of oil and oil-based products and could reasonably be expected
to discharge into navigable waters of the U.S. or adjoining shorelines. Therefore, the Project is required to
prepare and implement a SPCC Plan in accordance with U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA)
and Nevada Division of Environmental Protection (NDEP) regulations.

According to the criteria in 40 CFR 112.20(f)(1), the Project has determined the Project does not pose a
risk of substantial harm to the environment by discharging oil or oil-based products into or onto navigable
waters. See the Certification of Substantial Harm Determination included in Attachment 4. Therefore, the
Project response requirements in 40 CFR 112.20 and 112.21 do not apply.

1.3     Plan Availability

A complete copy of the SPCC Plan is maintained at the Project at the main construction trailer and is
available to all Project personnel. The SPCC Plan will be provided to local, state, and federal agency
personnel with jurisdiction for review during any inspection upon request.
