1.4   USEPA Plan Review and Amendment

In the event USEPA reviews the SPCC Plan during an inspection and requests to amend the SPCC Plan,
the Project has 30 days from receiving the notice from USEPA to file a written appeal. Otherwise,
amendments to the SPCC Plan will be completed within 30 days of receiving USEPA’s request to modify
the SPCC Plan, and implemented as soon as practical, but no later than six months.

1.5   Project SPCC Plan Review, Amendment and Certification

The Project periodically reviews and evaluates the SPCC Plan for modifications during construction. The
two types of amendments are described below.

Technical Amendments

These are changes in Project configuration which can include changes in design, construction, operation,
or maintenance that materially affects the potential for an oil or oil-based product discharge. This includes
(but not limited to) adding, removing or modifying containers; reconstruction, replacement, or installation
of piping systems; altering secondary containment structures; changes in product or service; changes to the
inspection program; and the use of new or modified industry standards.

Technical amendments to the SPCC Plan must be prepared and certified by a Professional Engineer (P.E.)
within six months of making these changes.

Administrative Amendments

These are changes to the SPCC Plan that do not affect the potential of the Project to discharge oil or oil-
based products and include (but are not limited to) personnel changes and changes in the name or contact
information of spill response or cleanup contractors.

Administrative amendments to the SPCC Plan will be completed by the Project and do not need to be
prepared or certified by a P.E.

1.6   Cross-Reference with SPCC Plan Provisions

This SPCC Plan may not follow the exact order presented in 40 CFR 112. Therefore, a regulatory cross-
reference of the SPCC Plan sections relative to the applicable parts of 40 CFR 112 is included in Attachment
5.

This SPCC Plan is in place to address risks associated with the volumes and range of products, anticipated
and likely to be added, during Project construction. Great Basin and its construction contractor(s) will
commit the necessary resources for implementation of the procedures described in this document. In
preparing the SPCC Plan, Great Basin is demonstrating its obligations to the public for responsible
environmental stewardship. The SPCC Plan also complies with the requirements of Great Basin’s Safety
Plan, ensuring employees are aware of applicable environmental issues and requirements, and to support
Great Basin in protecting the environment. Specifically, the SPCC Plan describes oil and other hazardous
material products and quantities typically found on pipeline construction projects, potential for discharge
of oil products, spill prevention measures, inspection and training requirements, and spill response and
notification procedures.

3.0 Spill Prevention
3.1     Containment and Diversionary Structures

SPCC-regulated equipment with oil-storage capacities of 55 gallons or greater are provided with
appropriate containment or diversionary structures capable of containing oil and oil-based products and
preventing offsite discharge. Appropriate containment can be passive (e.g., impervious dikes, berms or
retaining walls; drip pans; containment pallets) or active (e.g., spill response).

3.2     Project Security

3.2.1    Perimeter Fencing

Each laydown yard will be fenced, and access will be controlled by a locked gate.

3.2.2    Oil Pump Starter Controls

Fuel pumps will be locked from unauthorized use.

3.2.3    Loading/Unloading Connections

Filling of ASTs will be conducted during working hours and will be supervised by project personnel.

3.2.4    Lighting

All laydown yards will be lit at night to prevent vandalism and assist in the detection of oil spills and leaks.

3.3     Loading/Unloading Racks

The Project does not have any loading/unloading racks.

3.4     Field Erected ASTs

The Project does not have any field erected ASTs.

3.5     Conformance with Other Regulations

The Project will coordinate with the vendors to ensure they understand the Project layout and the protocols
for loading and unloading products and liquid transfer activities and will verify that vendors have the
necessary equipment to respond to a spill during these operations. Vendors will comply with all applicable
U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT) regulations.

In the event of a reportable release, Great Basin will provide the NDEP with the proper notification.

3.6     Management of Oil Storage

3.6.1    Drainage from Secondary Containment

Prior to drainage of retained stormwater from secondary containment, the accumulated precipitation is
inspected for visible sheen to ensure that its presence will not cause a discharge of oil.

3.6.3   Bulk Storage Containers

Tanks and containers will remain closed when not in use. Spill pans will be used during refueling and
maintenance activities to prevent any release from reaching the ground surface. A standard filling
procedure will be developed and adhered to by the construction contractor. Spill kits will be readily
available during vehicle maintenance activities and at all laydown yards.

The construction contractor will maintain spill kits at the site for containing incidental spills. Typically, a
spill kit is capable of cleaning a 5- to 25-gallon oil spill. Spill kits will be located near the oil containing
storage and equipment. Other absorbent materials, such as straw bales and absorbent clay, will be stored
on site in quantities necessary to respond to a spill event.

Aboveground Storage Tanks

ASTs with a shell capacity of 55 gallons or greater and holding oil or oil-based products are listed in Table
2-1. AST material and construction are compatible with the material stored and conditions of storage, such
as pressure and temperature.

ASTs are provided with secondary containment sized for the contents of the largest single container and
sufficient freeboard to contain precipitation. Secondary containment is sufficiently impervious to contain
discharged oil.

ASTs are inspected on a regular schedule in accordance with industry standards. Inspections of tank
supports and foundations are part of the inspection process, and the outside of tanks are frequently inspected
for signs of deterioration, discharges, and accumulations of oil inside secondary containment areas.

ASTs are engineered or updated in accordance with good engineering practice to avoid discharges and are
provided with direct visual gauges to prevent overfilling.

Mobile / Portable Storage Containers

Mobile or portable oil storage containers, including drums, totes and trailer- or truck-mounted fuel tanks
with a capacity of 55 gallons or greater, are listed in Table 2-1. Containers are compatible with the material
stored and conditions of storage, such as pressure and temperature. They are positioned to prevent
discharges and are provided with secondary containment sufficient to contain the contents of the single
largest container plus sufficient freeboard for precipitation.

Containers are inspected on a regular schedule in accordance with industry and regulatory standards.

Underground, Partially Buried and Bunkered Metallic Tanks

The Project has no underground, partially buried or bunkered metallic oil storage tanks.

4.2     Personnel Training

All employees handling fuels and other hazardous materials will be properly trained in spill response
procedures. Key personnel who will assume responsibility for the spill response procedures will be trained

procedures, emergency spill response procedures, and spill history. Training will be scheduled and
conducted by the Environmental Manager or designate prior to the initiation of construction to assure
adequate understanding of employee responsibilities. The topics to be addressed at the briefing will include

      1. SPCC Plan contents;

      2. Locations of oil and chemical storage;

      3. Possible equipment failure and malfunction;

      4. Precautionary measures;

      5. Standard operating procedures in case of a spill; and

      6. Equipment, materials, and supplies maintained by the construction contractor and location for
         cleanup of a spill.

Good housekeeping is required of all employees in the work areas and in operations. Fuel areas will be
kept clear of combustible materials. Storage areas will be well maintained and clear of obstructions. Routine
visual inspection of oil-containing equipment will help detect issues early so that leaks can be addressed
promptly. Good housekeeping will reduce waste generation and reduce the potential for spills. Spill kits,
fire extinguishers, and other response equipment should be readily accessible and working properly. Well
maintained material and storage areas will reduce the possibility of stormwater contact with pollutants.

5.0 Spill Response
Spill prevention through adherence to the SPCC Plan is the best means for avoiding a spill. However, if a
spill occurs, prompt response to a spill will minimize the impact on the environment.

5.1     Spill Response Procedure

The following procedures will be used in the event of a spill:

      1. Immediately, upon recognizing a spill or result of a spill (e.g., soil stain or sheen on water), the
         observer is required to contact a member of the Spill Team to report on the location and other details.
         The Spill Team member receiving the report will notify the other members of the Spill Team along
         with any actions taken or directed at the time.

      2. If there is no threat to personal safety, the employee shall attempt to contain the spill to prevent
         entry of discharged oil, or other hazardous substance, into a storm sewer, a ditch, or any conveyance
         that eventually discharges to surface water. Equipment used to contain spills includes spill kits, sand,
         loose absorbent, weed-free straw, hay, and absorbent pillows.

      3. At the same time as containment is being carried out or as soon as possible after containment, the
         employee(s) should attempt to safely seal or otherwise stop the source of the spill. Common
         methods of eliminating a spill source include closing valves, leak stopping compound for pinhole
         leaks, plugging drains, constructing terrace dams or ditches, drum over-packs, deactivating pumps,
         and diverting flow to another pathway, if the alternative pathway does not allow the spill to enter
         waterways.

      4. Once the spill is contained and the source eliminated, the emergency response contractor shall
         collect the spilled material by the appropriate manner and place the material into secure containers.
         This may include skimming oil products off freestanding fluids or excavating soil within the spill
         area and placing fluids or soil into USDOT-approved containers.

      5. The area or surface in contact with the spilled material shall be decontaminated by an appropriate
         method that is permissible under local, state, and federal laws. The specific method used will
         depend upon the substance, the availability of permitted sewer discharge to a publicly owned
         treatment works, regulatory standards applicable to hazardous and toxic wastes, and other factors.
         The emergency response contractor will select the appropriate cleanup and decontamination
         method after determining the applicable facts.

      6. All spill material and debris will be managed in a manner that fully complies with applicable local,
         state, and federal laws regarding recycling or disposing of wastes. The preferred method is to
         recycle or reclaim materials from spills to minimize waste generation. Hazardous waste material
         will be placed in USDOT-approved sealed containers, labeled, dated, inventoried, and then staged
         for no more than 90 days. Hazardous waste containers will be disposed of in accordance with
         federal and state regulations and will be manifested and transported using permitted transporters to
         permitted treatment, storage, and disposal facilities. Great Basin will retain manifest records for a
         period of at least three years. Disposal will be conducted in accordance with applicable local, state,
         or federal rules.

1.0 Project Introduction
This Horizontal Directional Drill(ing) (HDD) Procedures and Mud Monitoring Plan (HDD Plan) was
prepared for the Great Basin Gas Transmission Company (Great Basin) 2028 Expansion Project (Project).
The Project consists of the construction, operation, and maintenance of approximately 207 miles of new
48-inch diameter natural gas lateral pipeline (Lincoln Lateral), approximately 25 miles of smaller diameter
natural gas lateral pipelines (Project Laterals), and associated infrastructure in Churchill, Humboldt, Lyon,
Pershing, and Storey counties, Nevada.

This HDD Plan describes the HDD operational procedures and environmental protection measures that will
be implemented during HDD activities, including mud monitoring and contingency planning in the event
of an inadvertent return. Prior to construction, this HDD Plan will be updated to include the results of HDD
feasibility studies based on geotechnical investigations and associated site-specific design at each HDD
crossing. Additionally, the HDD Contractor will be responsible for updating this HDD Plan with applicable
Safety Data Sheets for each HDD additive. A copy of this Plan will be available and accessible to all
construction personnel at each HDD crossing.

2.0 Description of Horizontal Directional Drilling Methods
HDD is a trenchless pipeline installation technique that uses a specialized drilling rig and associated
equipment to install a pipeline beneath the ground surface without excavating a conventional open trench.
The HDD process generally consists of three primary phases. First, a relatively small-diameter pilot bore
is drilled along a predetermined alignment between designated entry and exit points. The pilot bore is then
enlarged through one or more reaming passes until it reaches a diameter suitable for pipeline installation.
Depending on the diameter of the completed bore and the subsurface conditions encountered, the pipeline
may be installed during the final reaming operation or pulled into the completed bore as a separate step.

During HDD operations, the drilling equipment is used to establish and maintain the borehole along the
designed horizontal and vertical alignment. The drilling assembly incorporates mechanical and hydraulic
components that allow the bore path to be adjusted as needed. Instrumentation continuously provides
information regarding the position, depth, and orientation of the drilling head, allowing the operator to
monitor the bore and make steering adjustments to maintain the planned alignment and reach the designated
exit location.

Directional control is achieved using an offset section of drill stem, commonly referred to as a “bent sub,”
which positions the cutting head slightly off the drill string centerline. When the drill string is rotated, this
offset produces a change in the direction of the cutting head. To steer the bore, the operator orients the bent
sub toward the desired direction and advances the drill string without rotation, allowing the cutting head to
gradually deviate toward the intended alignment. When straight-ahead drilling is desired, the drill string
can be rotated while advancing.

4.0 Instrumentation
The HDD Contractor will maintain appropriate monitoring equipment throughout HDD activities to
accurately track the pilot bore alignment and depth, monitor axial and torsional loads on the drill string, and
measure downhole drilling-fluid pressures. Mud volumes will also be monitored throughout drilling to
identify and document any potential loss of drilling fluid.

Before HDD construction begins, this Plan will be updated to specify the equipment, instrumentation, and
monitoring procedures that will be used to obtain the required measurements.

Great Basin, the HDD Contractor, the Environmental Inspector (EI), and Federal Energy Regulatory
Commission (FERC) will have continuous access to the monitoring equipment and associated data. The
HDD Contractor will maintain instrumentation logs that document pilot hole progression, drill string axial
and torsional loads, drilling fluid discharge rate and pressure, and down-hole annular pressure monitoring
during drilling of the pilot hole (or provide alternative monitoring methods and/or best drilling practices to
ensure that the drilled and bored [reamed] holes do not become plugged with drill cuttings leading to
hydrofracture and inadvertent return) and will provide these records to Great Basin as part of the required
As-Built documentation within 30 days following completion of the Project.

5.0 Pre-Construction Geotechnical Investigation
Great Basin or its designated representatives will retain a qualified and experienced Geotechnical
Contractor to perform subsurface investigations at each HDD location. Investigations will include soil
borings and rock coring, where appropriate, to characterize the subsurface geology to the extent reasonably
practicable and provide information necessary to develop the HDD crossing design.

The Geotechnical Contractor will use the results of the subsurface investigations, together with guidance
provided in the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) publication, “Guidelines Installation of Utilities
Beneath Corps of Engineers Levees Using Horizontal Directional Drilling,” to establish allowable
downhole drilling-mud pressures for each HDD based on subsurface formation conditions (Formation
Pressure Limiting Factor).

The referenced USACE guidance establishes drilling-fluid pressure limitations based on soil conditions and
depth beneath flood-control levees and is intended to minimize the potential for inadvertent returns of
drilling fluid to the ground surface near levees. Although the Project does not involve crossings of flood-
control levees, the methodology will be applied to HDDs where appropriate to establish conservative
drilling-fluid pressure limits and reduce the potential for inadvertent surface returns.

Great Basin or its designated engineering representative will evaluate the geotechnical investigation results,
along with applicable HDD design experience, to develop the design for each crossing. Documentation for
each HDD crossing will include, as applicable, the following:

    •   Type of sampling equipment used for investigation;

6.0 HDD Site Preparation
Prior to commencing HDD, the entry and exit areas will be prepared to provide adequate space for drilling
equipment, support facilities, material handling, and safe access. The entry side will accommodate the
HDD rig and associated equipment used to initiate and advance the bore, while the exit side will provide
sufficient workspace for receiving the drill head, managing drilling fluids and cuttings, and completing the
pullback operation. Site preparation will be conducted in accordance with the approved HDD design,
project specifications, and applicable environmental and safety requirements.

If necessary, the HDD Contractor will prepare temporary all-weather vehicle access to the HDD entry and
exit sides. The HDD Contractor will also provide a level, hard standing work area for equipment ingress
and egress and for the drilling operation area. The work area prepared may generally include the following
items based on location.

6.1       Entry (Rig Side)

The entry side, or rig side, setup will be approximately 250-feet by 250-feet in size. Access will be either
an “all weather” matted road capable of withstanding heavily loaded transporters or utilizing existing
facility roads. The ground conditions around the HDD work area may utilize wooden construction or
similar mats if necessary.

A small drill pit (imperviously lined if required by permit) will be excavated around the drill hole to

(see additional equipment below).

6.2       Dead Man

The Dead Man comes with the drilling rig at the entry side. The Dead Man is typically 1 foot deep x 22
feet long x 5 feet wide and is the primary anchorage device for the operation. The excavation for the Dead
Man must be accurate and the top of the Dead Man must be flush with the ground. If additional anchorage
is needed, the mud tanks can be connected to the rear of the rig or anchor piles will be driven to provide
adequate stability. The anchorage must be rigid and must not pivot.

6.3       Exit (Pipe Side)

The exit side (or pipe side) setup will be similar in size and setup as the entry side except that this side will
normally not have a drilling rig. The exit side is where the pipeline will be welded into long sections to be
pulled in after the hole has been drilled and reamed to proper size. The equipment may include welding
equipment, pipe side booms, cranes, pipe rollers and supports, and other pipe handling equipment.

7.0 Safety Requirements
The HDD Contractor will perform the work in a manner to maximize safety and reduce exposure to
personnel and equipment to hazardous and potentially hazardous conditions, in accordance with applicable
safety standards. The HDD Contractor will develop and implement a Project-specific safety plan and will
conduct daily tailgate safety meetings with all on-site personnel.

The HDD Contractor will perform HDD operations in a manner that will minimize the movement of the
ground; prevent subsidence of the surface, structures and utilities above, or in the vicinity of the directional
drilling operations; and protect the integrity of the carrier pipe as it is installed.

7.1       Pre-Construction Training

Prior to HDD site set-up, HDD-specific implementation and safety training will be conducted for Great
Basin and HDD Contractor personnel, including EIs and FERC Compliance Monitors (if applicable). This
training will address all applicable environmental impact avoidance and minimization measures that will
be implemented during drilling. Each person involved in HDD operations should be familiar with the
locations of inadvertent return containment equipment and materials, and the specific procedures for
handling inadvertent returns. Training will occur once prior to construction, and on an as-needed basis if
determined appropriate by the EIs or FERC Compliance Monitors. The HDD Plan should describe the
frequency of training and any circumstances that would result in additional training. The HDD Contractor
will maintain a record of employee training detailing when training was conducted, material covered, and
employees in attendance.

8.0 Project Personnel
The HDD Contractor will maintain qualified and experienced HDD personnel to observe conditions that
may threaten the stability of the HDD path or cause inadvertent mud returns or mud loss. Project personnel
generally will include, but may not be limited to, the following:

      •    Construction Foreman;
      •    Drilling Engineer;
      •    Tracking Engineer;
      •    Mud Engineer;

    •   Rig Operator;
    •   Equipment Operator;
    •   Inspectors; and
    •   Laborers.

9.0 Hours of Operation
HDD operating hours are expected to be during daylight hours, working 10 to 12 hours per day on a seven-
day work schedule. When the pipe string is being pulled in, operating hours are normally continuous around
the clock until the pipe is completely pulled in. Hours of operation in this HDD Plan will be updated by
the HDD Contractor prior to construction, as needed.

10.0 HDD Procedures
HDD construction will be performed by the HDD Contractor in accordance with this approved HDD Plan,
Project specifications, applicable codes and regulations, and accepted industry practices. The HDD
Contractor will be responsible for determining the means and methods necessary to safely and successfully
complete the HDD installation.

HDD construction will generally proceed through a series of sequential activities, beginning with site
preparation and installation of the drilling equipment at the entry and exit locations. The HDD Contractor
will first drill a pilot bore along the approved alignment and profile while continuously monitoring the bore
location, depth, and drilling conditions. Once the pilot bore reaches the exit location, the bore will be
enlarged through one or more reaming passes to achieve the required diameter for pipeline installation.
Following completion of reaming, the pipeline will be assembled, inspected, and positioned for installation.
The prepared pipeline will then be connected to the drill string and pulled through the enlarged borehole
from the exit side toward the entry side. Upon completion of the pullback, the pipeline will be inspected
and the entry and exit areas will be stabilized, drilling fluids and cuttings will be managed appropriately,
and the work areas will be restored in accordance with Project requirements. Specifics are as follows:

10.1.1 Pilot Hole

The drill unit is placed at the entry hole and aligned with the direction of the drill path. The drill unit is
then elevated at the rear so that the entry angle conforms to the proposed drill profile. The rig is then
anchored in position, and the pilot hole operation begins.

The pilot hole operation is executed by using the selected cutting tool, the bent sub steering tool, and the
pressurized injection of the bentonite slurry. The drilling is carried out continuously in intervals of 30 feet,
equivalent to one length of drill pipe. The alignment and depth are checked and corrected, and then a new
length of drill pipe is added, drilled forward, and alignment checked until the end of the drill is reached.
The downhole drilling mud pressure will also be monitored and controlled to stay within the limits
recommended in the Geotechnical Report.

10.1.2 Magnetic Guidance System

A Magnetic Guidance System (MGS) probe and interface will be used to provide a continuous and accurate
determination of the location of the drill head during the pilot operation. The MGS will be capable of
tracking at all depths up to approximately one hundred feet in any soil condition, including hard rock. The

                                                                          2028 EXPANSION PROJECT

MGS will enable the driller to guide the drill head by providing immediate information on the tool face,
azimuth (horizontal direction), and inclination (vertical direction).

The MGS are generally accurate to +/- 2 percent of the vertical depth of the borehole at each position that
readings are taken at depths up to one hundred feet. Ferrous materials will not influence or affect the MGS
readings or accuracy.

As previously mentioned, the actual tracking method used will be identified by the HDD Contractor. The
equipment selected will be able to provide the same tracking information for depths involved.

The Contractor will utilize the downhole pressure tool to monitor any pressures that could cause a potential
inadvertent return.

10.1.3 Reaming

Once the drill bit exits at the prescribed location, the downhole assembly (drill bit, steering tool, etc.) will
be detached and a series of reamers are installed and pulled back along the pilot hole until the hole size is
large enough to pull the pipe through.

During the reaming process, bentonite slurry is pumped under high pressure through the drill string to the
reamer. The HDD Contractor will also run the downhole mud pressure monitoring tool on each of the
reaming passes to ensure that the pressure is within the limits specified by the Geotechnical Report.

Reaming operations will be conducted at the discretion of the HDD Contractor to ensure that the hole is
sufficient to accommodate the pull section.

Reaming operation diameters are typically limited to 1.5 times the service pipe diameter; however, to avoid
damage to the line pipe during installation due to design factors (i.e., soil conditions, project length and/or
alignment, soil strata, etc.) the HDD Contractor reserves the right to exceed the 1.5 factor.

When the reaming operation of the hole is completed, a “swab” or “barrel reamer” is pulled through the
hole. Drilling mud is pumped through the drill string to the reamer as it is pulled along the drill path. This
ensures the hole is prepared for the carrier pipe pullback.

Once the Drill Superintendent is satisfied that the hole is clear of obstructions, and conditioned, and is ready
for the pullback operation to begin, the pulling head which has been attached to the pipe to be pulled in, is
then connected to the drill string by a swivel, and the pulling operation is started. The swivel prevents the
carrier pipe from rotating in the hole during the pullback.

10.2 Testing, Inspection, Stress Loads, Buoyancy and Post Pullback

10.2.1 Testing and Inspection

The pipeline will be welded into long pipe strings prior to pulling the pipe through the borehole. All welds
will be visually inspected and X-ray tested. The weld joints will then be coated with a corrosion protective
coating and an additional abrasive resistant coating to protect the coating from abrasions as the pipe is
pulled through. Prior to pullback, the pipe strings will be hydrostatically tested. The entire length of the
pipeline coating will also be inspected to locate any defects in the coating and repairs made if necessary.

10.2.2 Buoyancy

To reduce friction at the crown of the pipe rubbing along the top of the drill hole due to the positive
buoyancy of the carrier pipe in the bentonite slurry, the HDD Contractor may use a polyvinyl chloride or
high-density polyethylene pipe inserted in the carrier pipe to inject water into the pipe to counteract the
positive buoyancy of the pipe. The inserted pipe allows the equalization of air pressure on either side of
the injected water column in the carrier pipe.

10.2.3 Pulling Loads

The HDD design will ensure that the maximum allowable axial tensile load imposed on the pull section
will be less than or equal to 90 percent of the pipe’s specified minimum yield strength. The HDD Contractor
will be required to ensure that this tensile load limit is not exceeded.

10.2.4 Torsional Stress

A swivel will be used to connect the pull section to the reaming assembly to minimize or eliminate torsional
stress imposed on the carrier pipe section.

10.2.5 Pull Section Support

The pull section will be supported on pipe rollers that are spaced appropriately to adequately support the
pipe during the pullback so that it moves freely, and the pipe is not damaged, kinked, or wrinkled.

10.2.6 Post Pullback

After the pipeline is installed, it will be hydrostatically tested to confirm that the strength of the pipe and
its welds were not compromised during pullback.

10.3 Drilling Fluids

10.3.1 Composition

Drilling fluids will be a mixture of bentonite, polymers, and any other additives to help with the drilling
procedures. The viscosity may be varied to best fit the soil conditions encountered as recommended by the
drilling HDD Contractor. The HDD Contractor will document the use of loss control materials and other
drilling fluid additives, including the quantity, timing, and location of use. This HDD Plan will be updated
prior to construction to include the Safety Data Sheets of each selected HDD additive.

The HDD Contractor will maintain monitoring logs of drilling fluid physical properties throughout drilling
activities (e.g., fluid weight, viscosity, sand content, additives, and pH).

The HDD Contractor will maintain mud pressures and flow rates during drilling operation to prevent
fracturing the sub grade material around and/or above the bore.

It is the intent of the HDD Contractor that their drilling operations will be conducted in a manner to provide
a stable borehole and prevent the discharge of drilling fluids to waterbodies or to the land surface due to
exceeding anticipated mud pressure limits specified by the Geotechnical Report.

The HDD Contractor will utilize the downhole pressure tool to monitor the mud pressures on the pilot and
the reaming process to prevent any inadvertent returns. The HDD Contractor will also monitor mud
volumes used to detect if mud loss is occurring. The HDD Contractor will patrol the HDD path and adjacent
areas for any inadvertent returns occurring and communicate this to the Drilling Superintendent.

The “Formation Pressure Limiting Pressures” for each HDD based on depth and soil composition will be
established with a safety factor of 1.5 applied to the pressures calculated by the Geotechnical Contractor
and provided in the curves or tables generated in the Geotechnical Report.

10.3.2 Water

Unless Great Basin has obtained permits to allow for the withdrawal from surface waters, the HDD
Contractor will supply water from other approved potable water source(s). Non-potable water may need to
be tested and/or treated prior to use in a hydrostatic test.

10.3.3 Re-Circulation

Recycled drilling fluid systems will incorporate linear motion shakers to adequately remove solids from the
drilling fluids. The HDD Contractor may provide other such drilling fluid handling equipment, as it deems
necessary to properly manage the drilling fluids and to minimize drilling related wastes.

The HDD Contractor will provide vacuum truck(s) or frac tanks that have sufficient capacity to collect and
transfer drilling fluids from the exit pit to the drilling fluid system, located at the drill entry, or to a disposal
site.

Although not currently proposed, if drilling fluid will be reused between HDD locations, the drilling fluid
will be tested prior to reuse in consultation with local and state agencies. Laboratory results of sampled
drilling fluid/source water for any inorganic and organic environmental contaminants will be retained.

10.3.4 Disposal

Disposal of excess drilling fluids will be conducted in compliance with all environmental regulations, right-
of-way, workspace agreements, and permit requirements. Drilling fluid disposal will be conducted in
accordance with the Project Disposal Plan (Appendix 1.D-9).

11.0 Mud Monitoring and Inadvertent Return Contingency
The HDD Contractor will employ best efforts to maintain full annular circulation of drilling fluids to reduce
the chance of inadvertent return of mud to the surface in locations other than at the entry and exit holes of
the HDD.

Control of drilling fluid returns at locations other than the entry and exit points will use the following
methods:

    •   All construction personnel will be briefed on what to watch for and will be made aware of the
        importance of timely detection and response to any release of drilling mud.
    •    The HDD Contractor will monitor the pressure tool to keep mud pressures at or below the formation
         limiting pressure specified for each drill to reduce the chance of inadvertent returns.

    •   The HDD Contractor will patrol the right-of-way and adjacent areas, observing the drill path of the
        HDD, especially at the current location of the drill head during the pilot hole and for each reamer
        pass. The HDD Contractor will document and log the personnel monitoring the HDD alignment,
        location along the HDD alignment visually inspected, time of the examination, and observations
        following each inspection.
    •   Construction personnel will have appropriate communication equipment (e.g., radio, cell phones)
        available at all times during installation of the directionally drilled crossing.
    •   If inadvertent surface returns of drillings fluids occur, they will be immediately contained with
        hand placed barriers (i.e., hay bales, sandbags, silt fences, etc.) and collected using pumps, as
        practical, provided by the HDD Contractor.
    •   If the amount of surface return is not great enough to allow practical collection, the affected area
        will be diluted with fresh water, and the fluid will be allowed to dry and dissipate naturally.
    •   If the amount of surface return exceeds that which can be contained with hand placed barriers,
        small collection sumps (less than 10 cubic yards) may be used.
    •   If the amount of the surface return exceeds that which can be contained and collected using small
        sumps, drilling operations will be suspended until surface return volumes can be brought under
        control.
    •   Unsuccessful drill holes will be abandoned and sealed. Grout will be pumped into the hole to
        completely seal and fill it, except for the top five feet where compacted soil will be placed in the
        hole. The area will be graded back to its original contour to the extent possible.
    •   Drilling operations may also be suspended if at any time the EI determines that the inadvertent
        returns are endangering environmentally sensitive areas or until the HDD Contractor can bring the
        mud release under control.
    •   The EI will immediately notify Great Basin in the event of any inadvertent return and make any
        required regulatory notifications.
    •   In the event of a mud release in an in-stream area, the HDD Contractor will document the release
        and implement installation of containment as needed to prevent solids propagation. The HDD
        Contractor will initiate immediate suspension of drilling operation if the released volume is
        determined to pose a threat to human health and safety.

In the event an inadvertent drilling mud return is observed during the crossing, the return will be assessed
to determine the amount of drilling mud being released and potential for the release to reach waterbodies
or wetlands. To measure the downhole mud injection volume flow rate, the HDD Contractor can use an
inline flow meter to calculate the flow rate in gallons per minute. Another method is to calculate by pump
size, diameter, and stroke, timed in revolutions per minute.

Mud returns can be calculated three different ways:

    •   Measure the volume of the excavated receiving pits or mud tanks.
    •   Calculate by tanker volume.
    •   Measure the intake volume of the first receiving tank on the cleaning unit.

Comparison of the injection flow rate and return flow rate can be used to determine mud loss to the
formations or possible inadvertent returns.

The HDD Contractor can use a mud balance scale to weigh the mud to determine the percentage of solids
in returns.

11.1 Containment and Clean-up Equipment

Containment and clean-up equipment will be made available at the HDD crossing location to ensure a
timely response. Equipment supplied by the HDD Contractor may include:

    •   Hay bales
    •   Push brooms
    •   Silt fence
    •   Pumps
    •   Plastic sheeting
    •   Mud storage tanks
    •   Shovels
    •   Vacuum truck
    •   Squeegees
    •   Light plant/generator

11.2 Clean-up and Disposal

The following clean-up measures are considered appropriate following an inadvertent release in an upland
or wetland area:

    •   Drilling mud will be cleaned up by hand using hand shovels, buckets and soft-bristled brooms as
        possible without causing extensive ancillary damage to existing vegetation. Freshwater washes are
        also to be employed if deemed beneficial and feasible.
    •   Containment structures will be pumped out and the ground surface scraped to bare soil; without
        causing ancillary damage to existing vegetation.
    •   Material will be collected in containers or roll off boxes for temporary storage prior to removal
        from the site.
    •   Potential for secondary impact from the clean-up process is to be regularly evaluated and clean-up
        activities terminated if physical damage to the site is deemed to exceed the benefits of removal
        activities.
    •   In general, no clean-up measures will be initiated for in-stream releases. If site-specific conditions
        are such that containment and clean-up may be feasible and beneficial, freshwater washes or other
        low-impact steps may be employed without undue disturbance to the stream banks and bed.

Final clean-up of the drill site will return the area as close as practical to pre-drill conditions. Additional
clean-up requirements may be stipulated by permit or right-of-way agreement. Drilling mud or other
materials collected during clean-up will be disposed of in accordance with the Project Disposal Plan (1.D-
9).

12.0 HDD Site Descriptions
12.1 Humboldt River 1

At the Humboldt River 1 HDD crossing, Great Basin plans to maintain a hand-cleared 10-foot-wide
vegetation clearing area and walking path between the HDD drill locations, as needed, to support HDD
activities. No vehicle travel will occur on the permanent right-of-way between the HDD drill boxes during
construction or operation. This area contains standing water and environmentally sensitive resources that
will be avoided. Accordingly, construction and operational activities within the area between the drill
locations will be limited to pedestrian access and other activities necessary to complete the HDD while
minimizing disturbance to sensitive resources.

12.2 Pitt-Taylor Diversion Canal

At the Pitt-Taylor Diversion Canal HDD crossing, Great Basin plans to establish a hand-cleared 10-foot-
wide vegetation clearing area and walking path for installation and management of the HDD guide wire.
Construction equipment will not cross the canal at this location. Instead, construction equipment will access
the north side of the crossing via TAR-035.200 and will travel around the canal to access the south side and
the applicable HDD drill location. For operations and maintenance activities, Great Basin anticipates using
the 50-foot-wide permanent right-of-way to provide access for routine inspections. A standard pickup truck
may be driven to the edge of the canal from both the north and south sides, subject to confirmation that
such access will not affect potentially sensitive resources adjacent to the canal. Based on the results of the
sensitive resources review, TAR-035.200 may need to be converted to permanent access for the application-
stage design to ensure adequate access for future inspection and maintenance activities.

12.3 Humboldt River 2

At the Humboldt River 2 HDD crossing, Great Basin plans to use a geolocating drill head to guide the HDD
due to the length of the crossing. Therefore, installation of a guide wire and associated vegetation clearing
between the HDD entry and exit locations will not be required. Construction access to the HDD drill
location may be provided from PAR-048.000 where it intersects the permanent right-of-way between the
HDD drill boxes. From this intersection, construction equipment may travel west along the permanent
right-of-way to access the applicable drill location.

12.4 Interstate-80 (Churchill)

At the I-80 HDD crossing, Great Basin plans to establish a hand-cleared 10-foot-wide vegetation clearing
area and walking path to support installation and management of the HDD guide wire. During HDD
construction, the access route extending from PAR-081.000 along the right-of-way, past the western HDD
drill box, and connecting to TAR-081.100 may be used as a loop route for trucks transporting drilling mud
and other materials associated with HDD operations. Great Basin is evaluating future operational access
requirements, including whether routine operations and maintenance activities will require vehicle access
along the permanent right-of-way to the edge of the I-80 right-of-way.

12.5 Hazen Drain (Canal)

At the Hazen Drain HDD crossing, Great Basin plans to use the full 50-foot-wide permanent right-of-way
to facilitate the movement of construction equipment through the area. Construction equipment is
anticipated to cross the canal using a temporary railcar bridge designed to span the canal without contacting
